doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Meeting Clive Davis and starting with Melissa Manchester
summary: After his first hit Clive Davis quizzed him, liked four of six songs he sent, and sent him to Melissa Manchester.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Okay. When you get contracted or hired to produce a record with a person you have never met, or I guess I should ask first, has that happened?
But you would end up meeting them way before you go in the studio.
That’s my question, like what’s the first interaction like?

A meeting. After I did “I Love the Night Life” the next person to call me was Clive Davis and flew me to New York and he quizzed me. He played me demos of songs. He’d play me records that they were getting ready to release. And he would be very specific. “Do you think this is a hit? Why or why not?” He was very specific and we were there hours the first time I met with Clive in New York. And we left after that first day and he said, “Put together some songs” he’s a song man to this day, he’s what 86 or so now, and still the chairman of SONY/BMG or whatever it is now. And he said, “Put together some songs and send them to me.” And I did. I got I think six songs together from the few writers I knew. A couple of guys in LA, one guy in Muscle Shoals. And I put together a reel to reel tape back then, it was before cassette, and sent him a reel to reel of six songs. And within a couple of days I get a call from a secretary saying, “Come to New York, Clive wants to meet with you.” I went to New York and out of the six songs I sent him he loved four of them. And if you’ve ever worked with Clive Davis, I didn’t know it then, but he could go through two hundred songs and turn them all down. He was so critical. He’s a real song man. Not a musician, but a song man and a record man. Anyway, we played the four songs and he was asking me my ideas about the production from the demos, the writer’s demos. And then he started playing me songs. And I’d say, “I hear that one, I don’t hear that.” Anyway at the end of that day he said, “I’m flying you tonight to Los Angeles to meet with Melissa Manchester to do her next album.” And Melissa was — I did, you meet — well I flew out and met with her manager at her manager’s house the next day. And thank goodness it worked. Our first album was © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

successful, and her second album. And we did a Christmas album in the late 90s. I mean we’re still friends. I just went to see her play a few months ago, a couple of months ago. We’re still great friends. But that’s usually how — you have to meet with them ahead of time to see if there’s a chemistry.
